title: Caro-Kann Advance: the defender's bishop and the ...c5 clock

difficulty.label: Caro-Kann player whose 3.e5 opponent has a plan

objective.summary: White gained space with 3.e5 and their preparation usually ends a few moves later. Get the light-squared bishop out BEFORE ...e6 locks it in, survive the lunges at it, and land ...c5 against the chain's base with your development ahead of theirs.

planClasses.label: Strike the base with ...c5
planClasses.description: In this pack the strike is prepared, not immediate: the bishop leaves c8 first, ...e6 solidifies, and only then does the c-pawn hit d4 — so the resulting open c-file belongs to pieces that are already out.

planClasses.label: Chip the head with ...f6 later
planClasses.description: The second lever, held in reserve for the middlegame once the king is safe. Nothing in this pack's spine plays it; the pack's job is to reach a structure where it remains available.

planClasses.label: The bishop leaves before the chain closes
planClasses.description: Position-specific to the Caro-Kann and the reason it exists as an opening: unlike its French cousin, the c8 bishop gets outside the pawn chain before ...e6. Every White lunge in this pack is an attempt to make that bishop a target instead of an asset.

annotations: The move the whole opening is for: the problem bishop exits before ...e6 shuts the diagonal. At your level this is also the most common choice by a wide margin — and everything White tries next is an attempt to punish it.
The restrained system: develop, castle, keep the space. This is where most club preparation for White ends — a setup, not a refutation — and your equalizing plan runs on schedule against it.
Now, with the bishop already outside, close the wall. The chain d5/e6 against d4/e5 is the structure this pack's shape reference describes; your c-pawn is the one that talks to its base.

White prepares to castle before meeting the break. This is the decision beat for Black: strike at once with ...c5, or develop a knight first? Both are authored thinking; the checkpoint asks you to commit.

The break lands with White's king still in the centre — one tempo earlier than White would like. The c-pawn has moved twice, which is the honest cost; the claim is that hitting the base before White finishes developing is worth it.
White reinforces the base and keeps the tension. Your choice now shapes the middlegame: increase the pressure with ...Qb6, resolve with ...cxd4, or develop and keep both options.

The pressure move: the queen adds an attacker to d4's defender count and eyes b2, which the c1 bishop just stopped defending. White must now spend a move on the queenside or accept the tension permanently — either way, your opening has done its job.
The lunge you must be ready for: h4-h5 means the bishop that just escaped will be asked where it lives. This is prepared-White territory — and it has a prepared answer.

Meet the flank pawn with a flank pawn. The bishop keeps f5-g6 as a home, White's g4 now costs a pawn structure to play, and the inserted pawns favour you in most endings because White's h-pawn advanced first. The cost: g5 is White's forever.
The Bayonet: the most direct attempt to make ...Bf5 a mistake. White gains kingside space at the price of every light square around their own king.

Step back and let the pawns overextend. On g6 the bishop still watches the b1-h7 diagonal, ...h5 comes next to ask g4 a question, and White's prep — which usually stops right here — has bought space it must now defend for the rest of the game.

checkpoints.label: ...Qb6 — the base is under siege with your king safe to castle
...h5 — the Tal lunge met, structure fixed
...Bg6 — the space is White's, the light squares are yours
You are past the authored line

deviations.note: 4...c5 strikes before ...e6, with the bishop already out. It is a real alternative order; the difference from the spine is that dxc5 now comes while your e-pawn still stands on e7, and regaining the pawn costs the tempo the spine's order saves. Play both and compare where the c-pawn's second move went.

5...Nd7 develops first and keeps ...c5 in hand — the patient order. It concedes White one free developing move; whether the break is better prepared or merely later is exactly the comparison this checkpoint exists for.
5...Ne7 heads for f5 or g6, keeping the f-pawn free for a later ...f6 chip. Slower against the castled-and-ready plan, but it is the move that keeps BOTH levers alive longest.

6...cxd4 resolves the tension into piece play against d4. This is main-line theory in its own right; what you give up is the standing threat, which was taxing every White move. Choose it when White's setup is finished, not before.
6...Nd7 keeps every option and adds a defender to the queenside before committing the queen. The quiet handling of a position you are already comfortable in.

6...c4 closes the position and releases d4 from all pressure. The c-pawn spent two tempi to arrive at a square where it attacks nothing, and White's pieces are now free to turn to the kingside where the space already favours them. The break was your rent on the position; this move stops paying it.

feedbackClaims.text: After 3.e5 at the 1400/1600/1800 rating bands (Lichess blitz+rapid, 2024-01 through 2026-07), 3...Bf5 is Black's choice in 61.4% of 9,346,096 games and the immediate 3...c5 in 30.0% — the bishop-first plan this pack drills is the family's main road.

The Caro-Kann's identity in one rule: the light-squared bishop leaves the pawn chain before ...e6 closes it. Every White system against the Advance is priced by how hard it works to make that bishop a liability.

Against the restrained Nf3/Be2 setup, typical club preparation for White ends around move five or six; from the tabiya onward the better-understood plan, not the better-memorized line, decides the game.
